EVIDENCE REVIEW
Claim A: Leaders of the two parties in Congress are chosen through secret ballot elections within each party's conference or caucus at the start of each new Congress.
Claim B: Leaders of the two parties in Congress are elected every two years in secret balloting of their party caucuses.

REASONING
The core issue is determining which description more accurately reflects the constitutional and procedural process for selecting congressional party leadership. While both references involve secret ballot elections, Claim A provides more precise terminology by specifying that elections occur "at the start of each new Congress" - which aligns with the established constitutional procedure. Congress is formally organized at the beginning of each two-year term, making this the precise moment when leadership elections occur. Claim B's reference to "every two years" is less precise because it doesn't capture the procedural timing of when the new membership actually takes office and the legislative body is constituted.

SOURCE BASIS
The more authoritative source is the constitutional and procedural framework of Congress, where party leadership elections are specifically held at the start of each new Congress during the party caucus/conference meetings. This timing corresponds to when newly elected members are sworn in and the legislative body is formally organized.

CONCLUSION
Claim A is the more accurate description as it precisely identifies when congressional party leadership elections occur - at the start of each new Congress during party caucus meetings.
